title: AI art studio
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this workshop, students step into the role of "AI art directors" — they will use DALL-E, a text-to-image AI tool, to turn written descriptions (called prompts) into original pictures. Rather than drawing with a pencil, students will "draw with words," learning how small changes in language can dramatically change an image. By the end of the session, each student will have created a small personal gallery of AI-generated artworks and will understand, at a basic level, how AI image generators interpret text and turn it into visuals.

The activity is designed to build AI literacy through hands-on experimentation: students will notice patterns in what works and what doesn't, discover the AI's strengths and quirks, and reflect on questions of creativity, authorship, and bias in AI-generated art.

Tools & Resources

  • DALL-E (via ChatGPT with image generation): https://chat.openai.com — Free accounts have a limited number of image generations per day/hour; this can reset or run out mid-lesson, so plan accordingly.
  • Bing Image Creator (powered by DALL-E): https://www.bing.com/images/create — Free with a Microsoft account; uses a "boost" credit system that limits fast generations, but images can still be created (slower) after credits run out.
  • Craiyon (free, no login): https://www.craiyon.com — Good backup tool if internet is slow or accounts are unavailable; lower image quality but no sign-up needed.
  • A shared document or slide deck (Google Slides/Docs) for students to paste their prompts and screenshot their images for later review.
  • Projector or shared screen for teacher demonstration before students work individually or in pairs.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Open the chosen AI art tool (e.g., Bing Image Creator or ChatGPT) on the projector and explain: "This is an AI that turns your written descriptions into pictures. We call these descriptions 'prompts.'"
  2. Demonstrate with a simple prompt: "A red bicycle parked under a mango tree". Generate the image live and discuss what the AI got right or wrong.
  3. Show how adding detail changes the result. Regenerate using: "A red bicycle parked under a mango tree, in the style of a watercolour painting, warm afternoon light". Ask students to compare the two outputs.
  4. Introduce the "prompt formula": Subject + Setting + Style + Mood/Lighting. Write this formula somewhere visible for reference.
  5. Have students log in (individually or in pairs) to their assigned tool.
  6. Give students their first guided prompt to try: "A lion wearing sunglasses, sitting on a rooftop in Nairobi, cartoon style, sunny day". Let them generate and view the result.
  7. Ask students to write their own original prompt using the prompt formula, generate the image, and save/screenshot it.
  8. Have students generate at least 2 variations of their original prompt (changing style, mood, or setting) to see how the output changes.
  9. Ask each student to choose their favourite image and write one sentence explaining why the AI's interpretation surprised them or matched their expectations.
  10. Bring the group back together to share 3–4 favourite images on the projector, reading the prompts aloud before revealing the image.
  11. Close with a group discussion using the questions below.

Example Outputs

  • Example 1: Prompt: "A giraffe reading a book in a library, digital art style" — produces a whimsical, colourful image of a giraffe with glasses holding an open book, surrounded by bookshelves. Shows good understanding of combining subject + action + setting + style.
  • Example 2: Prompt: "A futuristic matatu flying over Nairobi at sunset, in the style of a comic book" — produces a vibrant, localized image blending familiar Kenyan context with sci-fi elements. Demonstrates creative combination of local culture and imaginative "what if" thinking.
  • Example 3 (comparison set): Same subject ("a cat drinking tea") generated in four styles — realistic photo, watercolour painting, pixel art, and pencil sketch — shown side by side. Demonstrates understanding that style keywords significantly change the output while the subject stays recognizable.

Facilitation Tips

  • Pacing: Spend no more than 10 minutes on the live demo — students learn fastest by trying prompts themselves. Reserve at least 25–30 minutes for hands-on generation.
  • Free-tier limits: Warn students in advance that they have a limited number of image generations. Encourage them to plan/write their prompt in a doc first, then generate, rather than generating impulsively and running out of credits.
  • Common confusion: Students often expect the AI to read their minds. Reassure them that vague prompts produce vague or strange results — this is a teaching moment about clear communication, not an AI failure.
  • Handling odd or "wrong" outputs: If the AI produces something inaccurate (e.g., wrong number of fingers, garbled text, mismatched objects), use it as a discussion point rather than an error to hide — ask "why do you think that happened?"
  • Sensitive content: Remind students that these tools have content filters and will block certain prompts (violence, real people, etc.). If a prompt is blocked, ask students to rephrase rather than try to bypass the filter.
  • Grouping: Pairing students on one device can reduce the load on free-tier limits and encourages discussion about word choice.
  • Internet issues: Have Craiyon (no login, browser-based) ready as backup if the main tool is slow or blocked by school firewalls.

Discussion Questions

  • What is a "prompt," and why does the wording of a prompt matter so much to the AI's output?
  • How do you think the AI "knows" what a lion, a mango tree, or a watercolour style looks like?
  • Can you think of a time today when the AI misunderstood your prompt? What might have caused that?
  • Is the image the AI created "art"? Who do you think should be credited as the artist — you, the AI, or both? Why?
  • AI image generators are trained on millions of real images made by human artists. What are the benefits and possible concerns with that?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Generate the same subject in 3 different art styles (e.g., cartoon, realistic, watercolour) and write one sentence comparing the results.
  • Medium: Create a short 4-image "story" using prompts that build on each other (e.g., a character's journey from morning to night), keeping the character consistent across prompts.
  • Hard: Design a prompt for an image that represents an abstract idea (e.g., "friendship," "hope," or "climate change") without directly naming it in an obvious way, then present the image to the class and have them guess what abstract idea it represents.
